transcript:
Meeting header: 2027-10-05 15:00 UTC | Duration: 58m | Attendees: Sasha, Diego (Redwood) - Maya, Liam, Priya (Orion)

[00:00] Sasha (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick check - recording on my side, recording?
[00:04] Maya (Orion): Yeah recording's fine.
[00:07] Diego (Redwood SE): Great, I'll jump into the demo - high level we'll show JSON mode / structured output, function/tool-calling, and how Console + Optimize help tune cost/latency.
[00:18] Liam (Orion): Perfect. We're most interested in reliably getting typed JSON back from the model and hooking it into our enrichment pipeline, plus any guardrails.
[00:26] Sasha: Awesome, that's exactly what we've prioritized for this session. Quick round of intros - Maya, you're leading the ML effort?
[00:31] Maya: Yup, head of ML, building analytics pipelines. Liam handles infra, Priya is on security/compliance.
[00:39] Sasha: Cool. On our side I'm AE for the account and Diego is the SE who worked on similar integrations.
[00:45] Diego: Jumping in - here's the demo link to the Console screens, I'll share it in chat: https://redwood.ai/console-demo (note: placeholder).
[01:03] [01:00] Diego (Redwood SE): Ok switching to Console - first thing, JSON mode. You can upload a JSON schema that defines the exact fields, types, and nested structures you need. We then run the model with a schema enforcement layer and a guardrail that tries to coerce/repair invalid outputs.
[01:20] Maya: When you say repair, does it rewrite the response or fail the call? We need deterministic behavior for downstream parsing.
[01:27] Diego: Good question. There are two modes - strict and best-effort. In strict mode the call will return a structured failure if the model can't meet the schema. In best-effort mode it attempts to coerce values (e.g., parse numbers from strings) and attaches an annotations object with "repair_reason" and probability scores. We'll show both.
[01:48] Priya (Orion): Who owns the annotations? Are they stored in the same transcript logs and do they contain PII?
[01:56] Sasha: Logs and annotations follow your retention policy - hosted defaults can be 30/90/365 days; with Dedicated/Private you control retention and logs are write-to-customer KMS if needed. We'll include the SOC2 packet in the follow-up.
[02:10] [02:00] Diego: Alright demo - sample prompt: "extract invoice line items and amounts" then expected schema with items: array of {description:string, qty:int, price:float, tax:float}.
[02:28] [02:25] Speaker 1: (snip) Diego pastes example prompt into playground.
[02:35] Diego: Running with hosted small model first to show iteration speed. Here's the raw LM output - it's messy: missing fields, prices as text. Now switch to JSON mode with schema enforcement.
[02:50] [03:00] Diego: See now we get a typed JSON blob, values coerced, and an annotations section: {"repairs": ["price parsed from '$12.00'"], "confidence": 0.86}.
[03:10] Maya: That looks useful. In production we don't want heuristic repairs hiding bad extractions. Is there a way to surface those rows for manual review?
[03:18] Diego: Yes - Console's routing lets you send low-confidence or repaired items to a human-in-the-loop queue or to a fallback model variant. You can also tag responses so downstream pipelines skip automated ingestion on flagged entries.
[03:31] Liam: What's the overhead of running strict validation? Latency wise.
[03:36] Diego: Validation itself is lightweight; most latency is model inference. In our tests strict mode adds ~10-40ms depending on schema complexity. More significant is whether you run a verification pass with a second prompt or a tiny verification model - that adds token cost and latency. Optimize helps with batching/kv-cache to offset cost.
[03:58] [04:00] Sasha: We also have Dedicated pools for predictable throughput. If you need single-digit tail latency for sync APIs, Dedicated or a warmed pool is the way to go.
[04:10] Maya: We run inference as part of our synchronous API - SLOs around 300ms p95. Do you have customers with similar needs?
[04:17] Diego: Yes - retailers and analytics shops. For 300ms p95 we usually recommend model distillation/quantized variants + aggressive batching/bounded latency config. We can show a config with max_batch_wait and token limits.
[04:32] [05:00] Speaker 2: slight crosstalk.
[05:12] Diego: Now showing function/tool calling demo - we'll map detected entities to our enrichment service via a function schema. This is the 'tool-calling' capability where the model returns a function name and JSON args and we call an internal service.
[05:28] Diego: Example: model returns "upsert_invoice_line" with args {"invoice_id":"INV-123","line_items":[...]} and our runtime can call a webhook or your internal service. You can configure retries, idempotency keys, and response transforms in the Console.
[05:45] Maya: So can we restrict which functions models can call? We want to avoid accidental exfiltration or calls to privileged endpoints.
[05:51] Diego: Absolutely - that's part of the guardrails. You define an allowed functions list per route. The model can't call other functions. We also support a dry-run mode that shows intent without invoking the function.
[06:07] Priya: For compliance, we need audit logs of every function call and the inputs. Are those logged and can they be redacted?
[06:14] Sasha: All calls are logged in the trace. With Private deployments you can keep audit logs on-prem; with hosted we offer configurable redaction rules and KMS encryption for sensitive fields. We'll include sample audit logs in the security packet.
[06:29] [07:00] Diego: Switching back - here's a live example where the model chooses the wrong enum for "payment_method". We configure a schema enumerations list and set fallback policy to either default, ask clarification, or fail.
[07:44] Maya: Clarification flow - can that be an automatic follow-up question issued to the end user or does it need app logic?
[07:51] Diego: Console can orchestrate simple clarification prompts automatically (templated). For more complex flows you integrate via function-calling: the runtime returns a clarification payload that your app surfaces to users.
[08:08] [08:15] Liam: About performance - curious how KV cache interacts with function-calling. If the model uses context from earlier tokens, does that break idempotency for function args?
[08:22] Diego: Good nuance. KV cache stores past attention states to speed autoregressive decoding; it doesn't alter the determinism of returned JSON schema. However, we recommend canonicalizing inputs for function calls and using idempotency keys when exactly-once is required. Optimize can detect repeated prompts and suggest cache-friendly batching.
[08:48] Maya: Can you show the Optimize recommendations for our kind of workload - many small invoices, high QPS but small token counts per call.
[08:56] Diego: Sure - Optimize suggests: enable prefix caching for repeated invoice headers, set a small max_batch_wait (e.g., 10ms) to avoid latency spikes, and consider a quantized model for the low-token case. It also runs simulated cost vs quality graphs - I'm sharing the Optimize snapshot: https://redwood.ai/optimize/overview (placeholder).
[09:22] [09:30] Speaker 3: (typing) Sasha posts link to SOC2 summary: https://redwood.ai/security/soc2 (placeholder).
[09:35] Priya: On encryption - do you support customer-managed keys (CMK) across hosted and dedicated?
[09:41] Sasha: Yes, CMK via KMS for Dedicated and Private. Hosted supports encrypt-at-rest with Redwood KMS; we can enable BYOK for enterprise contracts.
[09:51] Maya: About data residency - we have EU customers only, so need EU region processing.
[09:56] Diego: We have EU regions and support VPC Private deployments in AWS eu-west-1; for strict residency Private on-prem is also an option.
[10:10] [10:00] Diego: Now demoing a multi-step extraction - we run an initial parse to produce structured JSON, then a verification pass using a small instruction-following model to check for schema violations. Watch the logs: you can see a verification step that returns "row_3: failed", we route that to HITL.
[10:34] Maya: Nice. How do you measure regression? We train new model variants often.
[10:40] Diego: Console integrates with evaluation suites - you can run evals on a prompt set and get quality delta alerts. We tie rollouts to those evals so you can prevent deploying models that degrade extraction quality.
[10:58] [11:00] Liam: Ops question - what's the deployment path for Dedicated? We need to understand provisioning lead time and cost model.
[11:05] Sasha: Dedicated is reserved capacity with monthly commitments; provisioning timeline is usually 2-6 weeks depending on region and GPU inventory. Diego can follow up with an example Sizing worksheet.
[11:18] Diego: I'll attach a Sizing worksheet after. For initial POC we recommend hosted with an isolated tenant and then move to Dedicated once throughput/latency needs are validated.
[11:30] Maya: For the POC, we'd like to run 10k invoices/day through Redwood for 2 weeks. What's a rough cost estimate?
[11:37] Sasha: Ballpark depends on model choice - using a quantized 7B variant optimized via Optimize is often cheapest; I'll include a cost estimate spreadsheet.
[11:44] [12:00] Diego: Demo note - there's occasional transcription/human error in examples, but the runtime will show exactly what was sent to the model and the raw tokens returned.
[12:12] Priya: Regarding SSO - SAML ok? We need group-mapping for RBAC.
[12:18] Sasha: Yes SAML/SCIM supported for Enterprise. RBAC policies can be set per-route and per-environment.
[12:28] [13:00] Diego: Quick discussion about error modes - we surfaced three: validation-fail, repaired-with-annotation, and system-error. You can map each to a different downstream behavior.
[13:42] Maya: Good separation. For legal audit we need a schema-versioned record of the model used, prompt, and schema for each extraction.
[13:51] Sasha: We have immutable request traces with model hash, prompt, schema version, and route. Those are accessible via the Console and exportable.
[14:05] [15:00] Speaker 1: (brief silence)
[15:06] Diego: Showcasing sandboxed function-calling - we can run tool calls in a simulation mode so you can test flows without hitting production endpoints.
[15:19] Liam: That helps for integration testing. Do you have SDKs for our stack - we use Go and Python.
[15:24] Sasha: SDKs for Python, Go, and Node - code samples in the repo. We'll share a repo link.
[15:35] [16:00] Maya: A couple of edge cases - nested arrays with optional subfields sometimes trip up models. Any recommended schema patterns?
[15:43] Diego: Flatten where possible, add explicit nullability, and prefer enums for small categorical sets. Use post-parse validators as a second line. We can share example schemas.
[15:56] Priya: About redaction - if an invoice contains SSN or PII, can Redwood automatically redact sensitive fields before logs are stored?
[16:03] Sasha: Yes, redaction rules can be regex-based or field-focused; with Private you can run regex redaction on-prem. We'll include examples.
[16:16] [17:00] Diego: Wandering into a technical corner - for best latency/throughput, use fused kernels and optimized compilation paths; our runtime picks kernels based on sequence length. For invoice workloads with short contexts, kernel selection is critical.
[17:37] Maya: Do you support quantization-aware model variants?
[17:41] Diego: Yep - 4-bit/8-bit quantized variants are available, and Optimize will recommend quantization profiles per workload.
[18:00] [18:30] Speaker 4: (laughs)
[18:32] Diego: Quick note on canary rollouts - you can do percent-based rollouts tied to eval metrics. If extraction F1 drops by X, auto-rollback.
[18:45] Maya: That automation would save ops time.
[18:50] [20:00] Sasha: Time check - about 25 minutes left. Anything we should deep-dive on?
[20:12] Maya: We want to see the verification logs and the exact audit format for legal. Also the cost calc.
[20:20] Sasha: We'll include both in follow-up. Diego, can you run the perf baseline with their sample set?
[20:27] Diego: Yes - I'll coordinate with Liam after the call for access.
[20:34] Liam: Will share a small S3 bucket with sample invoices and a short script.
[20:40] Priya: And I'll compile a list of security questions - auth, logs, KMS, and data residency.
[20:45] Sasha: Great. Couple more quick demos - showing fallback to a smaller quantized model when primary is overloaded; you can route by latency or cost.
[21:02] [22:00] Diego: Here's an example policy: prefer model A for high-confidence extracts, else fallback to model B then queue for HITL. Policies are first-class in Console.
[22:25] Maya: One last ask - can we get a demo of the function-calling dry-run for our enrichment endpoint?
[22:31] Diego: Yes, we'll set that up as part of the POC.
[22:36] [25:00] Speaker 1: (silence)
[22:40] Sasha: Wrapping up - recap and next steps: share recording, security packet, sizing worksheet, cost estimate, and run a benchmark with their sample set.
[22:52] Maya: Sounds good.
[23:00] Liam: Thanks all, talk soon.
[23:05] Priya: Thanks.
[23:09] Diego: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the benchmark.

End of transcript.

References / Links shared in chat: https://redwood.ai/console-demo (placeholder), https://redwood.ai/docs/structured-output (placeholder), https://redwood.ai/security/soc2 (placeholder), https://redwood.ai/optimize/overview (placeholder).
